lessonRef.subject: financial-literacy
lessonRef.unitTitle: PF6 — Fraud, Scams, and Consumer Protection
lessonRef.title: Independent application A: verifying a request independently

objective: Learners apply an independent-verification method, ignoring any contact information supplied in a suspicious message and instead using a separately known trusted source, to three fictional scenarios of increasing subtlety, ending with a scenario that looks legitimate but still fails independent verification.
scenario: This task never asks the learner for any real account or personal information. Every scenario below is fictional and constructed for practice only, so the learner can build the habit of verifying independently before it matters in a real situation.
safetyNotes: This task teaches independent verification; it never collects any real account or personal information.
The correct move for any real suspicious request is always independent verification through a separately known source, plus telling a trusted adult.
materials: the three fictional scenarios on this task sheet

tasks.directions: Fictional Scenario A: a text message claims to be from a delivery company, saying a package cannot be delivered, with a link to 'reschedule and confirm payment details.'

prompts.text: Describe the independent-verification step you would take instead of clicking the link, and explain what makes it independent.

tasks.directions: Fictional Scenario B: an email appears to come from a fictional bank the learner's family actually uses, with the bank's real logo, asking the learner to 'confirm your account by replying with your login information.'

prompts.text: Does the presence of a real, correct-looking logo make this request safe to respond to?
choices: Yes, a correct logo makes it safe
No, a logo alone does not make it safe

prompts.text: Describe the independent-verification step you would take for Scenario B instead of relying on the logo.

tasks.directions: Fictional Scenario C: a phone call appears on caller ID as the learner's actual school, and the caller asks to confirm the family's address and a parent's phone number 'to update records.'

prompts.text: Does a caller ID showing the correct name guarantee the caller is who they claim to be?
choices: No, caller ID can be faked

prompts.text: Describe the independent-verification step for Scenario C, naming specifically where you would find the trusted contact information instead of using anything from the call itself.

tasks.directions: State the general rule across all three scenarios.

prompts.text: Write the one general rule that applied to all three scenarios, regardless of how legitimate the message, logo, or caller ID looked.

remediation: If a learner treats a correct logo or caller ID as proof of legitimacy, reteach with a single concrete fact: both are easy to copy or fake, so neither can ever substitute for looking up contact information independently, from a source the learner already trusted before the message arrived.
extension: Have the learner research, with an adult, one real reported example of caller-ID spoofing or logo-copying fraud and summarize, in writing, how independent verification would have caught it.
